summary: Specifies how to use several elliptic curve cryptography Brainpool curves for authentication and key exchange in TLS. It gives implementers a way to use these curves where they are required or preferred.

plainLanguage.summary: Secret codes are made with special math shapes. This says how a secure web connection can use one more family of shapes.

questions: how to use brainpool for key exchange
subtitle: Using secure, verifiable elliptic curves for encrypted web connections.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 supported elliptic curves, but only some curve families were defined for TLS negotiation. Organizations in some regions needed alternative curves that were verifiably secure.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how to use three ECC Brainpool curves (generated through a pseudo-random process and tested against standards from ISO, ANSI, and NIST) in TLS for authentication and key agreement.
tldr.outcome: TLS implementations can now negotiate Brainpool curves as an alternative to other elliptic curves, with test vectors provided to verify correct implementation.

today: RFC 7027 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 4492 by defining how to negotiate Brainpool curves in TLS, and the curves remain available for implementers that need or prefer them.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ECC Brainpool curves are sets of elliptic curves defined in RFC 5639. They are generated in a verifiably pseudo-random way and meet security requirements from ISO, ANSI, NIST, and the Standards for Efficient Cryptography group. RFC 4492 already allowed these curves to be used in TLS certificates for authentication, but it did not define how to negotiate them during a TLS handshake for key exchange.

This RFC adds the missing step: it specifies three Brainpool curves that can be negotiated when two parties set up a TLS connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Some shapes are known to be safe for secret math. This says how a secure connection can ask for those shapes during the setup handshake.

sections.title: Brainpool Curve Types for Negotiation
sections.content:
The RFC defines three Brainpool curves that can be negotiated in TLS using NamedCurve identifiers: integer values in the TLS handshake that identify which curve the parties agree on.

The three curves are brainpoolP256r1 (assigned value 26), brainpoolP384r1 (assigned value 27), and brainpoolP512r1 (assigned value 28). The numbers at the end (256, 384, 512) refer to the bit length of the curve: larger curves offer stronger security. These curves are suitable for use with both TLS and Datagram TLS (DTLS, the version of TLS for unreliable connections like UDP).
sections.plainLanguage: Three shapes get ID numbers so both sides of a connection can say which shape they want to use: a smaller one (256 bits), a medium one (384 bits), or a larger one (512 bits).

sections.title: Registration with IANA
sections.content: IANA, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, maintains a registry of TLS curve identifiers. This RFC registers the three Brainpool curves in that registry with their assigned values: brainpoolP256r1 as 26, brainpoolP384r1 as 27, and brainpoolP512r1 as 28. All three are marked as suitable for use with DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The official registry of internet numbers records these three shapes and their ID numbers so no two things get confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The overall security of TLS communication is limited by the weakest cryptographic part used. To achieve maximum security when using Brainpool curves, all related choices matter: the key derivation function, the symmetric encryption algorithm and key length, the message authentication algorithm, and the signature algorithm and hash function should all be chosen according to recommendations from NIST Special Publication 800-57 and RFC 5639.

Private Diffie-Hellman keys should be selected with the same bit length as the order of the base point of the curve and with maximum entropy. Implementations using elliptic curve cryptography can be vulnerable to side-channel attacks: implementations that use twisted curve arithmetic for efficiency must take special care, as the special parameters of the twisted curve may make it harder to protect against such attacks. General guidance on protecting elliptic curve implementations is available in publications from the German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) and in the textbook Guide to Elliptic Curve Cryptography.
sections.plainLanguage: Using a strong shape is not enough; every other part of the code lock must also be strong. Be careful that secret math operations do not leak information through timing or other side effects.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content: Appendix A provides test vectors for Diffie-Hellman key exchanges using each of the three curves. These are examples where two parties (A and B) each create a secret key and public key, then compute a shared secret. The test vectors give the exact numbers: the secret keys, the public key coordinates, and the resulting shared secret value. Implementers can use these to verify that their code correctly performs the elliptic curve operations. Test vectors are provided for the 256-bit, 384-bit, and 512-bit curves.
sections.plainLanguage: The document includes worked examples showing what the math produces: if you start with these numbers, you should end up with those other numbers. This lets you check that your code is working right.
